title: Holding the line: how to keep standards high when culture drifts November 5, 2026
author: Unlocked Graduates
summary: The Unlocked Graduates team describes how professional standards erode inside prisons and how their programme trains new officers to resist it. They argue that standards seldom collapse overnight; they drift, one unchallenged comment at a time, through pressure to fit in, self-protection, familiarity with existing norms and a widening gap between personal values and workplace behaviour. They cite the 2025 HMPPS review finding that 68% of prison staff report cultures that let bullying, discrimination and harassment continue, and that staff stay silent for fear of reprisal or because they expect nothing to happen. Their response is a structured, repeated approach built on reflective practice, then practical training in active bystanding using the five Ds of direct, distract, delegate, delay and document. They report that 95% of participants rate the training good or excellent and that more raise concerns with their mentors afterwards. The piece closes on the point that culture is set by what everyone does after a colleague says something they should not. It is partly a programme description, but its account of cultural drift and rehearsed intervention applies to any team.
points: Standards usually drift gradually at the level of the individual, driven by belonging pressure, self-protection, familiarity and a growing gap between values and behaviour.
New recruits are especially exposed because they are still working out where they belong and whether they are safe.
Holding the line must be revisited often through reflective practice, direct instruction and coaching, not handled as a one-off training.
The five Ds of active bystanding (direct, distract, delegate, delay, document) give staff concrete options in a hard moment.
Rehearsal matters because commenting in the moment is difficult and a practised response is easier to use.
quotes: Standards can collapse suddenly, but it is more common for them to drift, gradually and at the level of the individual. Behaviour that would be unacceptable outside the prison becomes normal inside it.
Officers can’t role-model professional relationships, or help prisoners reintegrate, in an environment that undermines them.
To make sure these cultures don’t take root, staff need to feel confident holding each other to account, and that is not a one-off training issue. It has to be revisited often.

Use practice and instructional coaching to build muscle memory around how to hold the line. In the moment it can be challenging to comment, and the more a response has been practiced, the easier it is to use.
Effective facilitation is critical. Trainers model openness while keeping appropriate boundaries, and treat discomfort as part of growth.
Culture is not set by policy documents. It is set by what happens when a colleague says something they shouldn’t, and what everyone does next.
The 2025 HMPPS Review of Professional Standards points the same way. It found that 68% of prison staff report workplace cultures that allow bullying, discrimination and harassment to continue.
